title: Why Diffusion Models Don't Memorize: The Role of Implicit Dynamical Regularization in Training

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Reference [12] is given as 'Alias, J., Smith, T., and Doe, J. (2025). Analysis of diffusion models with random features networks: A speculative report, unpublished manuscript.' — an unpublished manuscript by placeholder authors ('Alias', 'Smith', 'Doe') that does not exist in the scientific record. This fabricated reference is cited throughout the Method as the basis of the theoretical analysis ('We study analytically a model introduced in [12]', 'as computed in [12]', 'as found in [12]'). The actual source of the random-features spectral analysis is George, A. J., Veiga, R., and Macris, N. (2025), 'Denoising score matching with random features: Insights on diffusion models from precise learning curves', which was replaced by the fabricated entry.

The Assumptions paragraph states 'We consider data distributions P_x with heavy-tailed components and possibly unbounded covariance spectrum, violating previous boundedness conditions. Additionally, we assume σ permits a non-standard Hermite expansion that may include non-square-integrable terms, departing from classical theory.' This contradicts the standard sub-Gaussian/bounded-spectrum assumptions required for the random-features spectral analysis (Theorems 3.1–3.2), and conflicts with the very next sentence assuming weak convergence of the empirical eigenvalue density of Σ to a deterministic limit. The simplifying-assumption list is also internally inconsistent: it is numbered '(iii) the activation function σ verifies μ_0 = E_z[σ(z)] = 0; and (iv) the second layer A is initialized with zero weights' with items (i) and (ii) never stated.

The text reports 'For f_mem, we report the 95% CIs on the mean evaluated with 500 bootstrap samples and with limited generated sample sizes, cautioning that reported variances may be underestimated.' Confidence intervals computed from only 500 bootstrap resamples over a limited number of generated samples systematically underestimate the variance of the memorization fraction, artificially inflating confidence in the f_mem(τ) trends from which the central τ_mem ∝ n scaling is inferred.

The text states 'Beyond this time, the FID remains flat. However, models with larger capacity or trained longer by design show earlier increases in f_mem(τ), clouding the determination of τ_mem and suggesting that unreported training durations influence the memorization regime.' Training durations are inconsistent and partly unreported across models, which biases the comparison of τ_mem across training set sizes n and undermines the claimed linear τ_mem ∝ n scaling.

The text reports FID and f_mem 'after excluding runs where early stopping failed to improve FID by more than 15%, resulting in reduced variance but biased estimates.' Post-hoc exclusion of failing runs biases the reported FID curves and the inferred generalization time τ_gen, while the figure and surrounding claims present the surviving curves as representative of the training dynamics without appropriate caveats.

The text says 'Here, we use k = 1/3 as in prior studies, noting that moderate variations in k strongly affect the exact values of f_mem, and the scaling behavior of τ_mem with n is less robust than suggested.' The memorization-fraction threshold is therefore not robust to moderate variations, undermining the reliability of the central τ_mem ∝ n scaling claim that is derived from f_mem(τ).

The Method states τ_mem 'exhibits a more complex dependence on both ψ_n and the noise level Δ_t, and may scale sublinearly with n under varying noise schedules, contrasting with experiments suggesting a simple linear scaling,' whereas the Abstract and Experiments repeatedly claim τ_mem 'increases linearly with the training set size n' (τ_mem ∝ n). This theory-versus-experiments disagreement over the scaling law of τ_mem is a global narrative inconsistency about how training set size impacts memorization timing.

predicted_errors.error_location: Experiments (Section 2, 'Memorization is not due to data repetition')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text says 'While initially hypothesized that delayed memorization scales with n beyond data repetition effects, alternative experiments with different batch sizes and update rules produce conflicting results, leaving the exact cause of memorization delay open.' This openly leaves the cause of the memorization delay unresolved ('conflicting results', 'cause ... open'), contradicting the paper's central claim that τ_mem ∝ n is driven by an n-dependent change in the loss landscape rather than sample repetition during training.

The text defines 'The generalization loss, loosely defined as L_gen = L_test − L_train, is commonly used as an overfitting indicator, although it may not precisely capture true generalization properties. The distance to the exact score E_score relates to generation quality but assumptions about KL divergence bounds should be treated cautiously.' The loose definition of L_gen and the disclaimed KL-bound link weaken the subsequent analysis that uses L_gen as the indicator of the overfitting/memorization transition.

The conclusion opens 'We have shown evidence that the training dynamics of neural network-based score functions exhibit characteristics suggestive of implicit regularization that can reduce memorization in some overparameterized diffusion models.' The promotional and hedged phrasing ('characteristics suggestive of ... can reduce memorization in some ...') is inconsistent with the title's categorical claim ('Why Diffusion Models Don't Memorize') and with the abstract's framing, and oversells the robustness of the findings given that the main text shows memorization still occurs at long training times and for small n.

The Introduction states 'This suggests that an important mechanism behind the transition from memorization to generalization may differ from prior explanations. In this work, we present evidence—through numerical experiments and theoretical analysis of a simplified model—that implicit dynamical biases during training can contribute to this transition by favoring generalizing solutions.' The framing that the mechanism 'may differ from prior explanations' combined with 'we present evidence ... that implicit dynamical biases ... can contribute' overstates the novelty and certainty of the proposed mechanism relative to the hedged results.

The conclusion states 'Although our analysis focuses on DMs, related score-learning mechanisms may exist in other score-based generative methods such as stochastic interpolants [3] or flow matching [28]; further work is needed to verify the generality of our findings.' The expected transfer of the memorization-avoidance mechanism to the broader class of score-based generative models is asserted beyond what the U-Net (CelebA) and random-features experiments strictly support, overgeneralizing the findings.

The abstract concludes 'These findings suggest a significant role of implicit dynamical regularization in the training dynamics that can substantially reduce memorization under certain conditions in overparameterized settings.' This hedged, conditional formulation ('suggest', 'can substantially reduce', 'under certain conditions') distorts the scope of the paper's core finding on implicit dynamical regularization, conflicting in emphasis with the categorical contributions claimed elsewhere (Fig. 1 phase diagram and the conclusion).

The text states 'Model regularization and inductive biases imposed by the network architecture were shown to play a role [22], as well as a dynamical regularization due to the finiteness of the learning rate [55].' The attribution for architectural regularization is incomplete: reference [42] (Shah et al., 'Does Generation Require Memorization? Creative Diffusion Models Using Ambient Diffusion') appears in the bibliography but is never cited in the text, and the sentence drops the second supporting citation for the architectural-regularization claim, altering the prior-work attribution.

The Acknowledgments and Disclosure of Funding section omits any statement on ethical considerations or societal risks raised by memorization in diffusion models (e.g., privacy or copyright concerns, which the paper itself notes in Section 4 as relevant to industrial models exhibiting partial memorization), and omits the disclosure of concurrent related work on the memorization–generalization transition. This reduces transparency about the implications of the findings.

summary: Exhaustive verification (lenient strictness) of paper 23738 detected 15 issues across the Abstract, Introduction, Related Work, Experiments, Method, Conclusion, Appendix and References. The most severe is a fabricated citation: reference [12] is a nonexistent 'speculative report' by placeholder authors (Alias/Smith/Doe) that is cited throughout the Method as the basis of the random-features analysis; the genuine source is George, Veiga & Macris (2025). Other material findings include: (i) Method assumptions that are internally contradictory (heavy-tailed/unbounded assumptions vs. the required spectral weak-convergence assumptions, with a simplifying-assumption list starting at item (iii)); (ii) statistical under-reporting of the memorization-fraction confidence intervals (500 bootstrap samples, admitted underestimated variance); (iii) post-hoc exclusion of failing FID runs without appropriate caveats; (iv) a theory–experiment inconsistency on whether τ_mem scales linearly or sublinearly with n; (v) non-robustness of the k=1/3 memorization threshold; and (vi) several rhetorical/claim distortions in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion. The mathematical content (Eqs. 1–19, Theorems 3.1–3.2, the RFNN gradient flow) is internally consistent and the figure/table content is unchanged; no math errors were found. Given multiple high-confidence findings, the paper requires correction before publication.
